Actually, he's probably being totally serious. Movies shot on film are traditionally done at 24 frames per second because the human brain can only perceive 10-12 actual images per second, so anything above this starts to create the illusion of motion. However, the human brain actually works asynchronously to perceive visual stimuli, so... higher frame rates are not actually wasted; they're just not really needed to create the illusion of motion either.

Tl;Dr: Film movies are shown at less than 30 frames per second, so it's a common misconception, and that person is probably serious.

First, while computers do execute some of the trading autonomously much of the time, there are still individuals inputting trades into the systems for the computers to execute when the trades are completed.

Second, I want to point out that while the markets do close, there are exchanges operating in a viable way 24/5. It's only about 2 hours from when the markets in one major financial center close until the ones in Asia open up, which are actually filled with some busy after-hours trading. And, before the Asian markets close, the European markets open. Then, the market in the major financial center opens again before the London markets close. The only time there are no markets open is on the weekends, well... except of course the markets in Asia are open before it's even really Monday in the US.

Finally, the individuals on the trading floor at a major stock exchange are trading large blocks of stock personally. Basically, the way it's set up... There are traders and market makers. If you're trying to buy a particular stock, you go near the market maker and call out that you're wanting to buy/sell a certain amount of stock. The other individuals there are likely looking to do the same and you may be able to make a deal with them rather than the market maker. Or even for larger amounts than you might've been able to do otherwise without moving the market. For instance, it might be that 1000 shares are available at $20, 1500 at $20.01, 700 at $20.02, etc... but, you're needing to move 100k shares. So, what do you do? Well, you talk to the other traders there and you might be able to get that abnormally large trade moved without pushing the price up as much as if you just took all the relatively small amounts of stock that were available on the market at that moment.

I'm an attorney, so I'm going to back this up. People often seem to think that undocumented individuals cannot receive benefits. Well, it's actually considered unconstitutional for a state government to deny benefits to someone based on immigration status. The federal government is absolutely allowed to, yes. Most government social programs are actually administered by state governments, but obviously there are exceptions - such as social security.

Do undocumented individuals pay into social security without receiving any benefits? Yes. But, I've also seen undocumented individuals who have stolen people's identities preventing those who are legitimately claiming social security disability from receiving their benefits. See, the tax agency and social security administration share information. If the tax agency sees you have reported income under your social security number, then the social security administration also sees you've been working. And, if you've been working, then you don't need that disability check, right? So, they can cut that check off while it's all being sorted out. It really sucks for someone who has a significant injury, put in years of working and paying taxes, probably fought to get the benefits in the first place, and now has to fight again because someone thinks it's okay to report income under their number.

Court hearings are generally open to the public. If you want to watch a proceeding, I would recommend calling the local courthouse to speak to a court administrator or clerk, then just go down there when you're told they are. Just explain what you want to do.

Just so we're clear, full-blown trials are relatively rare. Over 90% of cases will settle. You might need to attend 2-3 before you see a full final hearing, but you will likely be able to observe the more minor hearings along the way.

Also, most hearings are going to be bench trials. You don't see the full pageantry unless it's for a jury, and jury trials usually take 3 days or more.
